summary:
Gauteng stands under the national framework of South Africa. The province's own contribution to the evidence base is substantial: the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa, 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors', was conducted in 2003/04 by OUT LGBT Well-being with the University of South Africa Centre for Applied Psychology (Wells and Polders) under the Joint Working Group research initiative, with partner organisations including Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, the Gay and Lesbian Archive and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

The Love Not Hate campaign research of 2016, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being and hosted by the Gay and Lesbian Archive, records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have ever been done in South Africa: the 2003 study covering Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the national campaign study itself. Gauteng therefore carries one of the country's few provincial-level hate-crime measurements, though the data is now two decades old.

On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman from Soshanguve living in Winterveld, was attacked at a tavern in Tshwane at about 1:30 am. A man stated that gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live', smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, and said 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', cutting her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead; the wounds were stitched at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, and as of 6 January 2025 MambaOnline reported the case had shown no progress. This is the province's most recent documented trans-specific hate incident on record.

On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court in Johannesburg, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). The court found that the Department of Correctional Services committed unfair discrimination and harassment against a transgender inmate by refusing to let her express her gender identity and by denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, and ordered the Department to implement the required accommodations and to enforce its own standard operating procedures. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. The judgment demonstrates an operational Gauteng court remedy, under PEPUDA, for discrimination against a trans person.

The same judgment is the only documented determination of where trans prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence, is held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre: initially housed in the Medium A section where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing; later transferred to Medium C; and at the time of the judgment housed in C Single Section, a segregated or solitary-confinement unit of Medium C. Despite requesting a single cell she was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates, first two cisgender gay men and then one cisgender male, which the Department justified by overcrowding. The court found that the Department's standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing single accommodation, and ordered the Department to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and to enforce its transgender-inmate standard operating procedures.
tangentialFactors:
Gauteng's hate-crime evidence base is unusually deep for a South African province but thin by international standards: three quantitative studies nationally in more than two decades, one of them provincial and now roughly twenty years old. Absence of newer provincial measurement should not be read as absence of the underlying conduct.

The Mokoena judgment is a Gauteng High Court ruling binding on the Department of Correctional Services in that case; whether the Department's standard operating procedures are applied in other Gauteng correctional facilities remains untested in the reported record.
localsOnly:
Residents of Gauteng can invoke the Equality Court division of the Gauteng High Court in Johannesburg for discrimination and harassment complaints, as Mokoena did, with remedies including orders to implement accommodations and enforce departmental standard operating procedures.

Provincial advocacy and research infrastructure includes OUT LGBT Well-being, the Gay and Lesbian Archive, Triangle Project and Behind the Mask, which have jointly produced the province's hate-crime research.

Reporting pathways for assault run through local stations such as Dube Police Station in Tshwane; the Mokoena-era record shows case progress after charge opening cannot be assumed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Dube Police Station assault case opened by Aobakwe Mahlobo has since progressed, resulted in arrest or prosecution is unresolved in the sources available here; the latest sourced status is 'no progress' as of 6 January 2025.

The 2003/04 Gauteng hate-crime prevalence figures themselves are not reproduced in the available inventory, only the study's existence, methodology and authorship; current provincial prevalence of hate crimes against trans people is not sourced.

Whether the Department of Correctional Services has in fact complied with the Mokoena orders, including single-cell housing and enforcement of its transgender-inmate standard operating procedures across Gauteng facilities, is not sourced beyond the judgment text.
